markdownRemark.html:
Whenever I get satisfying results from an AI agent, I look back at the context I provided in the input. Most often it's not that the instructions were precise enough, but rather it feels like I defined good limits and still left space for the model to be "creative".

I'd been thinking of my prompts as requests, but the prompts that worked best weren't single direct orders but rather a set of rules: use these tools, follow this style, don't touch that folder, etc. Each rule removed a set of possible outcomes, and the result got better every time I specified more limits.

The painter picks the paint first

Let's look at how we, people make things in general. A painter doesn't start with every color that exists. They squeeze out five or six onto a palette, and that small set is a big part of why the painting looks like theirs. A musician picks a handful of sounds for an album and sticks to them for weeks. A sculptor chooses marble or wood, a chisel or a rasp, and those choices decide half the shape before the first cut.

None of these people feel trapped by their choices. The choices are where the style comes from. An artist with infinite options and no limits usually produces nothing, or produces mud.

Working with an AI model is similar. The painter starts with an empty canvas and adds. With a model, we start with a canvas that already holds every possible picture at once, and our job is to take things away until only the one we want is left. That's much closer to sculpting than painting, we're cutting away stone.

From instructing to designing space

For most of computing history, we told machines exactly what to do, step by step: load this file, compare these values, you get the idea. The computer did nothing we didn't spell out (for most of the time ;)).

Agents don't work this way, and trying to make them do so is exhausting. We can't list every step for "build a small web app for tracking eating habits." There are multiple steps and we don't know most of them in advance. That's the whole reason we asked the agent to do it for us :)

What we can do is shape the room the agent works in. Asking for React and Tailwind excludes Vue, Angular and hand-written CSS without mentioning them. When we tell it the API should be stateless and follow REST, we rule out a huge number of designs it might have wandered into. This way we tell the agent where to go.

I find this mental model comfortable to work with. I stop trying to predict every move and start asking a different question: what does the space look like where only good answers fit?

Managing the probability space

A language model works on likelihoods. Asking it something vague gives the most average answer it can find. The average is the safest bet when it knows nothing about what we want to create. That's why "write a blog post about productivity" gets us the same post everyone has already read.

Every detail we add shifts those odds. When we name our audience, the average moves. Handing it an example of our writing moves it again. It is usually enough to say which words we don't like and a whole family of bland answers drops out. I picture it as a cloud of possible outputs that gets smaller and denser with each rule I add, until most of what's left is close to what I had in my head.

So the rule I keep coming back to is simple. The more specific the limits, the more likely it is that I get results I wanted. A one-line prompt is a lottery ticket, but a prompt plus a tool list plus a style guide is closer to a recipe.

This also explains something that used to irritate me a bit. When an agent produced results way different from what I imagined to get, like an answer that was too long or requirements that were too complex, I'd blame the model. Now my first question is what I left open. Usually there's a door I forgot to close, and the agent walked through it.

The unified theory of constraints

By constraint in the article title, I don't mean a set of strict rules like "maximum 50 characters." I mean it much more loosely. Anything that pushes the agent down one path and away from the others counts.

The prompt itself is a constraint. A list of tools for a web app is a constraint. A page of architecture guidelines for an API server is... yes, a constraint. Acceptance criteria are a constraint too. Even the example files we drop into the conversation count, because the agent will lean toward whatever patterns it sees in them.

Once I saw it this way, all the separate tricks people share online started to look like one idea. "Give the model a role", "Show it examples", "Write a style guide", "Use a system prompt", "Give the agent only the tools it needs". These sound like five different techniques. To me they're the same move made five ways: narrowing the space until the good answer is the likely one.

The constrains stack. When I build an API server with an agent, I end up with something like this:

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  GOAL          specified endpoints exist, tests pass         │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  ARCHITECTURE  domain-driven design, strict types,           │
│                DAG modules structure, etc.                   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  TOOLS         Node, Express, PostgreSQL                     │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  PROMPT        build a small production API for a given      │
│                purpose                                       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The nice thing is that each layer can change without touching the others. If I swap Node and PostgreSQL for Python and MongoDB, the prompt, the philosophy and the goal stay exactly as they were. The agent adjusts because I changed one setting, and the rest of them are still there.

Managing constraints

If constraints are what make the results good, then they should be something more that one-off notes. A good set of API guidelines works for the next projects. A writing style guide I spent an evening on improves every piece of writing after it. Yet most of this work lives in a chat window and disappears when I close the tab. Next week I type a weaker version from memory.

Constraints should be treated like an artifact, a building block. We should store them, version and manage. Let's try them on real tasks and watch if an agent returns what we expect. If not, let's adjust them. We should keep the constrains somewhere easily to find, and share them with people who do similar work. Someone else can take our guidelines, change two lines for their team, and passe that version on.

We, software engineers already do this with code: nobody writes their own date library. We pull in one that thousands of people have tested already. I'd like the same for the things that shape agents. Picture starting a project by picking a tested set of architecture guidelines, a writing voice you trust, and a short tool list, instead of starting from a blank prompt box and hoping.

The human part

I write less of the actual code or text than I used to. What I do more is deciding what good looks like, and then describing the space where good is the only thing that fits.

It's the same craft the painter uses when choosing six colors out of hundreds, and it still comes from taste, experience and knowing what we want. The agent can give us every option in the world. Our job is to make it give us the ones we want.
